anchors.reason: The paper title and abstract explicitly describe and introduce the publicly available EEG dataset of 111 healthy subjects, matching the dataset's content.

metadata.methods_description: EEG data were recorded using a BioSemi ActiveTwo system with 64 electrodes positioned according to the extended 10-20 system (10-10). Four minutes of continuous resting-state EEG were acquired from each subject with eyes closed. Raw data signals were rereferenced to average reference without additional filtering. Derived cleaned data were preprocessed using a fully automated pipeline including artifact detection and channel interpolation, with results stored as EEGLAB .set files.

The inability of supervised EEG encoders to learn robust EEG patterns and their over-reliance on expensive signal annotations have sparked a transition towards general-purpose self-supervised EEG encoders, i.e. EEG foundation models (EEG-FMs), for robust and scalable EEG feature extraction. In this work, we conduct a review of ten early EEG-FMs to capture common trends and identify key directions for future development of EEG-FMs. Methods. citation_details.author: Chuanliang Han, Vincent C. K. Cheung, Rosa H. M. Chan
citation_details.abstract: Biological sex profoundly shapes brain function, yet its precise influence on neural oscillations was poorly understood. Despite decades of research, studies investigating sex-based variations in electroencephalographic (EEG) signals have yielded inconsistent findings that obstructs what may be a potentially crucial source of inter-individual variability in brain function. To address this, we analyzed five publicly available resting-state datasets, comprising EEG data (n = 445) and iEEG data (n = 103). Three age ranges were defined, young adult (YA, 18-30 years), middle-aged adult (MA, 30-55 years) and older adult (OA, 55-80 years). Our results revealed striking age-dependent sex differences: OA group exhibited robust sex differences, with males showing heightened low alpha (8-9 Hz) activity in temporal regions and attenuated low beta (16-20 Hz) oscillations in parietal-occipital areas compared to females. citation_details.author: Junhong Lai, Jiyu Wei, Lin Yao, Yueming Wang
citation_details.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals play a crucial role in understanding brain activity and diagnosing neurological diseases. Because supervised EEG encoders are unable to learn robust EEG patterns and rely too heavily on expensive signal annotation, research has turned to general-purpose self-supervised EEG encoders, known as EEG-based models (EEG-FMs), to achieve robust and scalable EEG feature extraction. However, the readiness of early EEG-FMs for practical applications and the standards for long-term research progress remain unclear. citation_details.abstract: Over time, pathological, genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors can age the brain and diminish its functional capabilities. While these factors can lead to disorders that can be diagnosed and treated once they become symptomatic, often treatment is difficult or ineffective by the time significant overt symptoms appear. One approach to this problem is to develop a method for assessing general age-related brain health and function that can be implemented widely and inexpensively. citation_details.title: Aperiodic and periodic components of resting-state EEG in primary insomnia
citation_details.author: Duo Bai, Yatong Guo, Simon Theodor Jülich, Xu Lei
citation_details.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Insomnia is one of the most prevalent health concerns within the general population, with a multitude of existing electroencephalographic (EEG) spectral studies supporting heightened levels of high-frequency EEG activity as an index of cortical arousal. Nevertheless, traditional spectral analysis has been limited by its inability to distinguish between aperiodic and periodic elements. In contrast, a novel method, Spectral Parameterization (SpecParam), can separate these components and reveal the neural mechanisms of cortical arousal.


METHODS
The aperiodic and periodic activities of 42 insomnia disorder (ID) patients and 45 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC) were evaluated during eyes-closed resting state. The associations between behavioral scales and aperiodic/periodic parameters were further examined to elucidate the underlying psychophysiological significance.


RESULTS
We found that the aperiodic exponent was diminished in the ID group compared to the HC group.

citation_details.abstract: Abstract Alpha rhythm (8-13 Hz), a key neural oscillation in the brain, plays a significant role in cognitive functions and reflects the brain’s excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) balance. This study investigates the dynamics of alpha rhythm across the lifespan, focusing on how E-I balance modulates alpha power and peak frequency, and exploring the distinct age-related and sex-specific patterns of alpha activity. Using a computational E-I model, we simulated the impact of different neuronal connections and E-I ratios on alpha rhythm characteristics. The results suggest that self-regulation primarily affects alpha power, while interaction between excitatory and inhibitory neurons influences both alpha frequency and power. citation_details.title: Spectral Differential Network Analysis for High-Dimensional Time Series
citation_details.author: Michael Hellstern, Byol Kim, Z. Harchaoui, Ali Shojaie
citation_details.abstract: Spectral networks derived from multivariate time series data arise in many domains, from brain science to Earth science. Often, it is of interest to study how these networks change under different conditions. For instance, to better understand epilepsy, it would be interesting to capture the changes in the brain connectivity network as a patient experiences a seizure, using electroencephalography data. A common approach relies on estimating the networks in each condition and calculating their difference. Such estimates may behave poorly in high dimensions as the networks themselves may not be sparse in structure while their difference may be. We build upon this observation to develop an estimator of the difference in inverse spectral densities across two conditions. Using an L1 penalty on the difference, consistency is established by only requiring the difference to be sparse. We illustrate the method on synthetic data experiments and on experiments with electroencephalography data.

citation_details.title: Beyond Phase Estimation: A Multidimensional Gating Framework for Robust Real-Time Closed-Loop Neural Stimulation
citation_details.author: Wenjia Zheng, Lu Shen, Biao Han
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Neural oscillatory phase is widely used as a control variable in real-time closed-loop stimulation, yet its validity under strict causal constraints and noisy conditions has rarely been systematically examined. We introduce a Multidimensional Gating Framework (MGF), a plug-in and estimator-agnostic module that determines whether phase information should be admitted into control by evaluating instantaneous amplitude, narrowband signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and spectral peak ratio (PR) within a strictly causal window. Using causal streaming replay on a public resting-state EEG dataset, we benchmarked Hilbert based phase estimation and endpoint-corrected Hilbert estimation with and without MGF. Among feasible subjects, MGF significantly reduced phase dispersion for both estimators, while robustly suppressing catastrophic phase errors. In contrast, ungated approaches exhibited systematic failures under the same conditions.

citation_details.title: Comprehensive methodology for sample enrichment in EEG biomarker studies for Alzheimer’s risk classification
citation_details.author: Verónica Henao Isaza, David Aguillón, Carlos Andrés Tobón-Quintero, Francisco Lopera, John Fredy Ochoa-Gómez
citation_details.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Dementia, particularly Alzheimer's disease (AD), constitutes a major global health concern, with AD accounting for approximately 70% of all cases. EEG-based biomarkers hold promise for early identification of individuals at risk; however, small and heterogeneous samples frequently limit generalizability. METHODS: An EEG-based sample enrichment framework was developed by integrating advanced signal processing, component-level feature extraction, data harmonization (neuroHarmonize), and Propensity Score Matching (PSM). EEG data from four independent cohorts were harmonized to reduce site-related variability while preserving covariates such as age and sex. Features including power, entropy, coherence, synchronization likelihood, and cross-frequency coupling were extracted from independent components. PSM was applied at 2:1, 5:1, and 10:1 ratios to expand and balance the control group (HC) relative to the Alzheimer's risk group (ACr), composed of PSEN1-E280A mutation carriers without cognitive symptoms. RESULTS: Sample enrichment through PSM improved classification accuracy, with decision tree models yielding values between 0.91 and 0.96. Higher enrichment ratios enhanced model stability and generalizability, as shown by learning curves and confusion matrices. Feature selection was based on model performance and effect sizes (Cohen's d). CONCLUSIONS: The proposed framework addresses sample size and variability constraints in EEG-based AD risk classification. SIGNIFICANCE: Harmonization and statistical balancing provide a replicable strategy for multicenter EEG studies targeting early AD detection.

citation_details.title: LEAD: An EEG Foundation Model for Alzheimer's Disease Detection
citation_details.author: Yihe Wang, Nan Huang, Nadia Mammone, Marco Cecchi, Xiang Zhang
citation_details.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive, highly accessible, and cost-effective approach for detecting Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, existing methods, whether based on handcrafted feature engineering or standard deep learning, face three major challenges: 1) the lack of large-scale EEG-based AD datasets for robust representation learning; 2) limited generalizability across subjects; and 3) difficulty in adapting to highly heterogeneous data. To address these challenges, we curate the world's largest EEG-AD corpus to date, comprising 2,238 subjects. Leveraging this unique resource, we propose LEAD, the first large-scale foundation model for EEG-based AD detection. Specifically, we design a gated temporal-spatial Transformer that can adapt to EEG recordings with arbitrary lengths, channel configurations, and sampling rates. In addition, we introduce a subject-regularized training strategy to enhance subject-level feature learning. We further employ medical contrastive learning for pre-training on 13 datasets, including 4 AD datasets and 9 non-AD neurological disorder datasets, and fine-tune/test the model on the other 5 AD datasets. LEAD achieves the best average ranking across all 20 evaluations on 5 downstream datasets, substantially outperforming existing approaches, including state-of-the-art (SOTA) EEG foundation models. These results strongly demonstrate the effectiveness and practical potential of the proposed method for real-world EEG-based AD detection. Source code: https://github.com/DL4mHealth/LEAD

citation_details.abstract: Reproducibility package for: The Geometry of Conscious States: Direction and Dispersion in EEG State Transitions Companion code for:Howie, S. J. (2026e). The Geometry of Conscious States: Direction and Dispersion in EEG State Transitions. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19600377 OVERVIEW This deposit is the single source of truth for every numeric result in the geometry paper. Each headline number traces to a specific script in analyses/ and a specific output file in outputs/canonical/. Running scripts/run_all.sh --stage analyze from a clean checkout reproduces every figure, table, and cited value from the deposited per-subject feature JSONs in outputs/. The paper treats conscious-state transitions as directions and dispersions in a five-dimensional state space whose axes are the framework's Phi components: I_A (interaction density), organization (1 minus normalized graph entropy), memory (I_M), recursive feedback I_R, and relative alpha power. I_R is the canonical normalized spectral radius of the thresholded Granger-causality graph. The central findings are the near-orthogonality of the sleep and propofol exit directions, the wider per-subject angular dispersion of the propofol pathway, and the equal-weights composite choice. DATASETS (about 314 subjects after QC; per-subject feature JSONs bundled) Sleep (ANPHY-Sleep, OSF thsqg), n = 28 — sleep exit (Wake to N3)Cambridge propofol (Chennu et al.), n = 19 — propofol exit (Baseline to Moderate)DS005620 (OpenNeuro ds005620), n = 20 — light-sedation hybrid exitSRM (OpenNeuro ds003775), n = 111 — normative healthy-adult baselineHBN (OpenNeuro ds005505), n = 136 — relative-alpha swap verification SELF-CONTAINED REPRODUCTION bash scripts/run_all.sh --stage analyze reproduces every cited value from the bundled per-subject feature JSONs in outputs/ (no external testsuite needed). Then: python scripts/verify_outputs.py re-derives every value in outputs/canonical/paper5_numbers.csv against its committed reference within tolerance and exits nonzero on any mismatch. The raw-EEG preprocessing in pipelines/ is optional and needed only to regenerate the feature JSONs from the source datasets listed in datasets/manifest.md. CONTENTS (selected) analyses/trajectory_geometry.py — group-mean 5D vectors, magnitudes, inter-paradigm angles.analyses/trajectory_stats.py — per-subject trajectory statistics and inferential outputs (bootstrap CIs, label-permutation p-values, dispersion-variance tests).analyses/angular_dispersion.py — per-subject trajectory dispersion.analyses/swap_effect_sizes.py — relative-alpha swap per-channel effect sizes.analyses/weighted_geomean_analysis.py — Fisher-LDA weights versus equal weights (characterization; equal weights are what the framework uses).pipelines/ — optional raw-EEG reprocessing per cohort._framework_core/ — shared constants, signal IO, and Phi-component computation.scripts/run_all.sh, scripts/verify_outputs.py — pipeline driver and numeric verification gate.outputs/ — bundled per-subject feature JSONs and canonical result tables. REQUIREMENTS Python 3.11 with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, and MNE (see environment.yml or requirements.txt). MNE is needed only for raw-EEG reprocessing; the analyze stage runs from the bundled feature JSONs. CROSS-DEPOSIT NOTE This deposit's _framework_core is the pre-retirement five-channel vintage (persistence I_M present), matching the geometry the paper analyzes. The Paper 4 deposit ships a same-named core that retired I_M to a four-channel Phi, so the two stamp different pipeline hashes and their raw Phi and C x 100 are not cross-deposit comparable. This deposit is internally self-consistent with its own core. VERSION v4 (2026): documentation hygiene only; no numeric or code-behavior change. Removed two dead references from the README layout and added the Phi-vintage cross-deposit caveat. Version 3 (May 2026) bundled _framework_core at the top of the zip, renamed the cohort feature JSONs to the series convention, and added the verify_outputs.py numeric gate. CITATION Software (version-independent concept DOI): 10.5281/zenodo.19600211Companion paper (concept DOI): 10.5281/zenodo.19600377

citation_details.title: 5D Conscious State Test Suite: Reproducibility Package for The Geometry of Conscious States
citation_details.author: Spencer Howie
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: Standalone reproducibility package for the manuscript "The Geometry of Conscious States: A Five-Dimensional Framework" (Howie, 2026, Zenodo, forthcoming). The code and committed feature data regenerate every numeric result cited in that manuscript — group-mean state vectors and magnitudes, inter-paradigm angles, per-subject trajectory dispersion statistics, the pooled-baseline Φ_ref calibration (n=67), and the equal-weighted versus Fisher-weighted geometric-mean comparison — from five publicly available EEG datasets: ANPHY Sleep (OpenNeuro ds003768, n=28) — endogenous acute exit Cambridge propofol (n=19) — pharmacological acute exit ds005620 light propofol sedation (n=28) — partial pharmacological exit ds003775 SRM normative (n=111) — pooled-baseline anchor ds005505 HBN (n=136) — eyes-open / eyes-closed developmental contrast used in the channel-substitution audit Running bash scripts/run_all.sh --stage analyze from the committed feature JSONs reproduces every canonical output; python scripts/verify_outputs.py numerically checks each of the twenty pinned values against the frozen reference in outputs/canonical/paper5_numbers.csv. Raw BIDS preprocessing (CAR re-reference, epoching, feature extraction) is also included under pipelines/ and is invocable if users want to replicate from raw data. The composite implemented is the equal-weighted geometric mean of five channels — interaction asymmetry, organizational specificity (1 − H_norm), inverse memory depth (1 − I_M), recursive integration, and relative alpha power — with the Consciousness Index reported as 100·Φ₅/(Φ₅ + Φ_ref). Canonical Φ_ref = 0.716. The implementation lives in analyses/_common.py. Full directory layout, dataset provenance, and per-number output mapping are documented in the deposit's README.md and MANIFEST.md.

citation_details.title: Code and trained models for: HC-Anchored Rank Normalization for Cross-Cohort EEG Classification of Alzheimer's Disease
citation_details.author: Spencer Howie
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: Cross-cohort EEG-AD classification pipeline accompanying Howie (2026g), "HC-Anchored Rank Normalization for Cross-Cohort EEG Classification of Alzheimer's Disease." What's included: Full preprocessing pipeline (10-20 channel selection, FFT resampling to 100 Hz, 30-second epoching, common-average referencing). Feature extraction for the canonical v2 17-feature pool (CHANNELS_4D + AP_TOPO + CONN_ALPHA + CONN_THETA) via a shared canonical ingest layer (_framework_core/) with cryptographic SHA-256 pipeline-version stamping. The legacy 15-feature v1 pool is preserved as core/feature_spec.py::ALL_V1_LEGACY for sensitivity-table reproduction. Per-cohort HC-anchored rank-based inverse-normal normalization, HC-covariance whitening, and Platt-scaled probability output. Bundled trained model (trained_model/trained_model.json) with v2 parameters (AUC 0.9476, BA 0.9362, sens 0.8824, spec 0.9900, PPV at 30% prevalence 0.9742, NPV at 30% 0.9515; classifier threshold tau = -2.3967; Platt a / b = 0.8202 / 1.3742) — direct application to new EEG without re-running training. Pre-computed 10,000-permutation LDA-target null on the v2 pool (in-pool AUC observed 0.9238, LOO 0.9102, LOCO 0.8382; all 0/10000 permutations greater than or equal to observed; p less than or equal to 0.0001 floor on each statistic). Three smoke tests in tests/test_canonical_pipeline.py confirm byte-identical pipeline output on a clean unzip. An 80%-coverage filter on sparse photic-driving features and a demographic deny-list (age, sex, MMSE) prevent label leakage. Reproducibility: The classification pipeline reproduces the paper's headline numbers byte-identically when run against the cited public datasets (ds004504, ds006036, ds003775, ds005385, BrainLat, MPI-LEMON age greater than or equal to 60 yr, figshare 5450293). README.md documents the full quick-start; CHANGELOG.md tracks v1 to v2 substantive changes; notes/RESEARCH_LOG.md preserves the development log for contex. License: MIT.

citation_details.abstract: Python test suite and intermediate results accompanying Howie (2026e), "The Geometry of Conscious States: A Five-Dimensional Framework." Self-contained reproducibility package for every numeric result in the paper: every figure, table, and cited value reproduces from the deposited per-subject feature JSONs by running `scripts/run_all.sh --stage analyze` on a clean checkout. Five EEG datasets (~314 subjects after QC), processed with the CAR-harmonized v1.2 pipeline and analyzed under the 5D state-geometry framework: Sleep (ANPHY-Sleep, OSF: thsqg) — n = 28; sleep exit(W to N3) Cambridge propofol (Chennu et al. archive) — n = 19; propofol exit (Baseline to Moderate) DS005620 propofol (OpenNeuro ds005620) — n = 20; light-sedation hybrid - SRM (OpenNeuro ds003775) — n = 111; normative healthy-adult baseline HBN (OpenNeuro ds005505) — n = 136; rel_alpha swap verification (EC vs EO) What's included: Pipelines (raw EEG to per-subject 5D features): reprocess_car_local.py: Sleep + Cambridge CAR + I_Preprocessing ds003775_reprocess.py: SRM normative baseline ds005620_reprocess.py: light-sedation reprocessing hbn_reader.py / hbn_reprocess.py: HBN developmental normative phi5_swap_committed.py: rel_alpha swap verification driver Analyses (committed feature JSONs to canonical numbers): trajectory_geometry.py: group-mean 5D vectors, trajectory magnitudes, inter-paradigm angles trajectory_stats.py: per-subject trajectory statistics, bootstrap CIs, label-permutation tests, leave-one-out sensitivity angular_dispersion.py: per-subject trajectory dispersion dispersion_pathway_figure.py: dispersion / pathway visualization weighted_geomean_analysis.py: Fisher LDA weights vs equal-weights comparison via log-space LDA swap_effect_sizes.py: rel_alpha-vs-I_P channel-swap per-cohort effect sizes (Cohen's paired d_z, four-cohort composite) Outputs: outputs/ _5d_car_data.json: per-subject 5D featurevectors for each cohort outputs/canonical/: every result cited in the paper as CSV / JSON / log; verify_outputs.py diffs a fresh run against this outputs/figures/: PNG and SVG figure outputs Series-wide compute primitives (_framework_core/) shared byte-identically with the empirical-paper deposits: pairwise Granger causality, GC matrix construction, transitive closure, spectral radius, all five Phi5 channels. I_R operationalization: the canonical normalized spectral radius rho(W) / rho_max of the thresholded Granger-causality graph. Reproducibility: run_all.sh runs the full pipeline (preprocess to analyze to verify); accepts --datasets and --analysis filters for partial re-runs verify_outputs.py reports "OK -- all canonical values reproduce within tolerance" on a clean unzip environment.yml (conda) and requirements.txt (pip fallback) pin dependencies manifests/ tracks every QC'd subject ID across the five datasets Data sources (downloaded separately, not redistributed): ANPHY-Sleep (OSF: thsqg) Cambridge propofol (Chennu et al. archive; access details indatasets/manifest.md) OpenNeuro ds005620 (light-sedation paradigm) OpenNeuro ds003775 (resting-state normative cohort) OpenNeuro ds005505 (HBN developmental cohort) License: MIT.

citation_details.title: Scalp EEG reveals functional dissociable aperiodic timescales in divergence of mental health
citation_details.author: Yuhan Lu, Hangze Mao, Xing Tian
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Understanding the divergence of mental health requires recognizing the brain’s real-time information processing. For example, aperiodic neural activity characterizing intrinsic brain dynamics is increasingly used as a biomarker in mental health, yet how its temporal complexity relates to mental deviations in ageing and disorders remains unknown. Here, using resting-state electroencephalography from approximately 1,700 participants across healthy, neurological and psychiatric disorders and chronic-pain cohorts, we show that the knee-like frequency structure recovered from individual spectra of neural activity converges into two reproducible, population-level temporal components. These slow and fast aperiodic timescales showed distinct functional profiles: the slow component remained stable across all states of mental health, whereas the fast component increased with healthy ageing, decreased in mental disorders and was unchanged in chronic pain. These findings establish that scalp EEG preserves functionally dissociable aperiodic timescales, possibly reflecting body-mind interactions, offering scalable, non-invasive temporal markers for quantifying divergent states of mental health.
